concepts.title: Social Structure: Stable Patterns of Relationships

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Social Structure: Stable Patterns of Relationships' refers to.
questions.a: Social structure refers to the recurring, organised patterns by which a society arranges its members -- families, castes, classes, offices and the expected relations among them. It is invisible as a thing yet visible in effects: it channels what people routinely do and constrains what they can do.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Social Structure: Stable Patterns of Relationships'.
questions.a: Society has a skeleton -- positions and relations laid out in advance -- and everyone is born into its frame.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Social Structure: Stable Patterns of Relationships' taught, and from which source text?

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Social Stratification: Caste and Class' refers to.
questions.a: Stratification is society's ranking of people into layers with unequal wealth, power and honour. Caste is ascribed at birth, bounded by endogamy, backed by ideas of purity and pollution, and traditionally unchangeable; class is based mainly on economic position, is theoretically open to mobility, and is reproduced through property and education rather than ritual.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Social Stratification: Caste and Class'.
questions.a: Caste fixes your floor at birth; class can shift with fortune -- both stack society into layers of unequal life chances.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Social Stratification: Caste and Class' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Social Processes: Cooperation, Competition and Conflict

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Social Processes: Cooperation, Competition and Conflict' refers to.
questions.a: Social life runs on recurrent processes of interaction. Cooperation joins efforts toward shared goals; competition is the rule-bound race for scarce goods where rivals chase the same prize; conflict is the collision where parties seek to nullify each other. Societies blend all three, often in sequence.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Social Processes: Cooperation, Competition and Conflict'.
questions.a: Working together, racing each other, clashing head-on -- cooperation, competition and conflict are society's three basic gears.
